newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's new leaders stumble into row with Cuba.
newsitem.headline: Spain's new leaders stumble into row with Cuba.

text.p: Spain's young conservative government appeared to have been caught completely off-guard on Tuesday when the centrepiece of its foreign policy blew up into a full-scale diplomatic crisis with Cuba.
"It's surprising," Foreign Minister Abel Matutes told reporters at a news conference called after Havana accused Madrid of meddling and rejected its new ambassador.
Earlier, when state radio called him for comment, Matutes was unable even to confirm Havana's withdrawal of its acceptance for new ambassador Jose Coderch.
In Havana, Spain's diplomats were literally caught napping.
"They got our (current) ambassador out of bed before dawn," a Spanish official told Reuters.

Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's six-month-old government has taken a colder approach to Cuba than its Socialist predecessor, the main departure in foreign policy. The change has clearly pleased Washington but angered Castro.
Cuba was particularly irritated by a Spanish initiative earlier this month to bring its 14 European Union partners in line with a united get-tough policy.
The Socialists, in opposition since May after 13 years in power, wasted no time accusing Matutes of having brought on a crisis that was fully predictable.
"You could see it coming," Jose Borrell, a Socialist member of parliament and a former minister, told reporters. "A diplomat must be diplomatic."
Sympathies for Cuba still run deep in Spain, which has traditionally maintained warm relations and close business ties with Havana.
Critics of the Cuba policy at home fear it will damage Spain's special status as the link between European and Latin America and compromise its business interests in the region.

Former Socialist Prime Minister Felipe Gonzalez taunted the government over its Cuba policy last week, saying Madrid's European Union partners would be only too happy to exploit any vacuum in economic ties.
Spain is a major investor in Cuba's private sector, notably in hotels and the tourism industry and in tobacco and cigar interests.
The Spanish proposal to the EU urges Cuba to move toward democracy and open a dialogue with the Roman Catholic Church while holding out increased cooperation with Europe as an incentive.
"Spain is certainly proposing to be a bit tougher than the European Union has been in the past," a European diplomat in Madrid said on Monday. "The general recommendations have been accepted."
Cuba objects to the plan, which it sees as an attempt to condition cooperation and mirror the aims of the United States.
Havana has also been angered by very vocal public criticism from Spanish leaders.
"I have nothing against Cuba, but everything against its regime," Aznar said at the Ibero-American summit in Chile earlier this month.
Madrid's words and deeds have clearly delighted Washington.

"We have watched with appreciation as that policy has unfolded in the last months and there is a considerable convergence between the Spanish policy towards Cuba and the United States'," U.S. ambassador to Madrid Richard Gardner said this month at a forum on U.S.-Spain business links.
Spain and the United States still disagree fundamentally on the approach to promoting democratic reforms in Cuba.

Spain, like the rest of the European Union, rejects a U.S. embargo on Cuba and the U.S. Helms-Burton Act, which gives Cuban-Americans the right to sue foreign companies that own or operate properties seized by the Cuban government.
